Subject: Marketplace onboarding - need clarity on SP vs Processor language for US addendum

Hi Logan —

Thanks again for the demo last week. As we start onboarding Brightlane into the Brightlane marketplace, our legal team has a few follow-ups about the US state privacy addendum: specifically whether Marketplace sellers that connect to Redwood via the marketplace are treated as separate controllers or whether Redwood's roles should be described as a service provider/processor for telemetry and transaction data.

Two asks to start: 1) can you confirm Redwood's proposed fallbacks for onshore processing for US-state restricted data (we saw notes in the console on onshore-fallback but need contractual language), and 2) a current subprocessor list for any marketplace-adjacent third parties (logging, analytics, billing). We attached a suggested redline from our side (Brightlane_DPA_Redlines_v3.pdf).

Ideally we can get a short mapping doc + a hit list of clauses Brightlane legal should accept vs escalate. Is Marissa on your privacy/compliance team the right person to take this?

Best,

Chrissy
Sr. Counsel, Brightlane Inc.

Subject: Re: Marketplace onboarding - need clarity on SP vs Processor language for US addendum

Chrissy —

Thanks for the note and the redline. Quick answers first:
- Redwood's default stance for marketplace integrations is to treat inbound customer data (i.e., Brightlane's customer records) as "service provider/processor" activity under CCPA/CPRA-style addenda when we process on behalf of the marketplace seller.
- For telemetry/aggregates where Brightlane is a buyer of marketplace analytics, we typically define a narrow "limited use" exception so we can operate caching, usage metering, and public aggregate reporting without re-identifying individuals.
- Onshore fallback: we support an onshore fallback commitment in the addendum (region=us) for categories flagged as restricted — this is typically a contractual appendix that references our Dedicated or Private deployment options and an operational timeline (30-90 days depending on capacity).

I'll loop in Marissa and Aditya to provide the formal mapping and subprocessor evidence. Can you confirm whether Brightlane wants the onshore fallback as a SLA-level obligation or as a best-effort? That will change the redline language.

Also: for the redline you sent, we have a single suggested edit on the "sale"/"share" definitions and one on telemetry anonymization thresholds (Marissa will propose exact language).

– Logan
Head of Marketplace Partnerships
Redwood Inference

Hi Chrissy —

Copying the compliance thread. I reviewed the redline and sketched a short mapping that should help your team triage clauses without escalating everything to the procurement table. Key points:

1) Role mapping table (summary):
- Marketplace seller data uploaded via API/tokens: REDWOOD = processor/service provider (limited to purposes in the order + ops).
- Marketplace aggregated telemetry derived by Redwood to power marketplace features: REDWOOD = controller for aggregated outputs only; we will provide strictly non-identifiable aggregates and advertise the transformations (e.g., 10+ threshold before publishing).
- Billing/chargeback events sent to our billing partner (Stripe): REDWOOD = processor; Stripe = subprocessors under Redwood.

2) Subprocessor evidence: attached is the current list — logging (Datapath LLC), observability (PulseStack), billing (Stripe), DocSign integrator (DocSign), and a transient CDN (EdgeFlare). We can produce SOC2 snapshots on request.

3) Onshore fallback: we will accept an addendum that commits to an onshore fallback within 60 days for flagged datasets if Brightlane purchases Dedicated capacity or accepts a fee for priority onshore migration. For free-tier hosted endpoints we propose a "best reasonable efforts" fallback. If you want SLA-level (financial credits) we'll need Dedicated capacity commit.

4) Suggested redline language: replace Brightlane's proposed "service provider" ambiguous clause with a two-paragraph binding definition: a) processing on behalf of the marketplace seller limited to order/ops, b) no sale or targeted advertising uses, c) narrow telemetry exception limited to aggregates and billing reconciliation. I'll paste the exact clause in my next message.

Please confirm which datasets you want flagged as "restricted" (e.g., PII emails, geolocation, purchase history) and whether your procurement team will accept the Dedicated/fee path for SLA onshore fallback.

Thanks,
Marissa Cole
Privacy & Compliance
Redwood Inference

Chrissy / Brightlane procurement —

Appreciate the specific restricted categories. We can support an SLA-backed onshore migration plan without an upfront Dedicated purchase but we will require a committed capacity ramp and a migration fee schedule; details below are a draft proposal you can share with procurement: 

- Commitment: Brightlane signs a 12-month addendum with committed QPS and a migration lead time (30 business days after activation).
- Financials: migration fee to cover priority onshore provisioning + reserved buffer (one-time, tiered by dataset size).
- Credits: if Redwood misses the 30 business day rehosting SLA we will provide a service credit equal to 10% of monthly committed fee for each week delayed (capped at 50%).

Subprocessor evidence: we will send a DocuSign package with the latest subprocessor register and SOC2 redacted snapshots. The drive link in this thread contains the marketplace dataflow diagram and the privacy mapping draft.

If this approach is acceptable, we will: 1) prepare a short addendum with the role mapping table and SLA appendix, 2) push the DocuSign evidence bundle, and 3) provide the standard subprocessor onboarding questionnaire for Brightlane to use on future marketplace sellers.

TL;DR: yes, we can do SLA-backed onshore fallback without Dedicated purchase if procurement signs the capacity/fee commitment.

– Aditya Rao
Director, Product Privacy & Compliance
Redwood Inference
